meta.description: Manual installation and configuration of NVIDIA drivers on a Proxmox VE 9 host, plus the LXC wiring needed to expose the GPU to one or more containers. Covers driver install, persistence service, optional NVENC patch and the per-container setup.

header.title: Installing NVIDIA Graphics Card Drivers on Proxmox VE 9 (manual procedure)
header.description: Manual installation and configuration of NVIDIA drivers on a Proxmox VE 9 host, plus the LXC wiring needed to expose the GPU to one or more containers. Covers driver install, persistence service, optional NVENC patch and the per-container setup.

intro.calloutBody: This is the manual procedure preserved as a reference. For most users the recommended path is the automated ProxMenux flow: Install NVIDIA Drivers (Host) in the GPUs and Coral-TPU menu, and Add GPU to LXC (or Add GPU to VM) for the per-guest wiring. The automated flow handles the same steps documented here (with extra safety checks: kernel-headers compatibility, IOMMU validation, VFIO conflict resolution). This page is for users who want to understand each command, or who need to deviate from the standard flow.
intro.targetNote: Targeted at Proxmox VE 9 (Debian Trixie). PVE 7 (Bullseye) and PVE 8 (Bookworm) are no longer covered.
steps: Prepare the Proxmox VE 9 host (blacklist nouveau, repos, prerequisites).
Install the NVIDIA driver on the host.
(Optional) Apply the keylase patch to lift the NVENC concurrent-session limit on consumer GPUs.
Wire the GPU into one or more LXC containers and install the matching driver inside each.

prepareHost.heading: 1. Prepare the host (PVE 9)
prepareHost.blacklistBody: Check whether the open-source nouveau driver is already blacklisted:
prepareHost.blacklistAdd: If blacklist nouveau does not appear, add it and reboot:
prepareHost.reposBody: Post-install tools may already have configured the repositories. Inspect the existing sources first and skip changes that are already in place; do not create duplicate entries.
prepareHost.reposOtherwise: Otherwise, on a vanilla PVE 9 install with no enterprise subscription:
prepareHost.reposPveBody: Make sure it contains the no-subscription source for Trixie:
prepareHost.reposPveCode:
Types: deb
URIs: http://download.proxmox.com/debian/pve
Suites: trixie
Components: pve-no-subscription
Signed-By: /usr/share/keyrings/proxmox-archive-keyring.gpg
prepareHost.reposDebianCode:
Types: deb
URIs: http://deb.debian.org/debian/
Suites: trixie trixie-updates
Components: main contrib non-free non-free-firmware
Signed-By: /usr/share/keyrings/debian-archive-keyring.gpg

Types: deb
URIs: http://security.debian.org/debian-security/
Suites: trixie-security
Components: main contrib non-free non-free-firmware
Signed-By: /usr/share/keyrings/debian-archive-keyring.gpg
prepareHost.updateHeading: 1.3 Update the system and install prerequisites
prepareHost.buildToolsBody: Install the build tools and kernel headers needed to compile the NVIDIA kernel module:
prepareHost.buildToolsCode:
apt-get install -y git
apt-get install -qqy pve-headers-$(uname -r) gcc make

installDriver.heading: 2. Install the NVIDIA driver on the host
installDriver.pickBody: Choose a driver branch that supports your GPU and running kernel. The newest branch may not support older GPU models; check NVIDIA’s supported-products list for the chosen release:
installDriver.nvencCallout: If you plan to apply the NVENC patch (step 4), verify the patch supports your chosen driver version first: <patchLink>github.com/keylase/nvidia-patch</patchLink>
installDriver.pickReplace: Replace latest.txt in the URL with the version number to find the installer file ending in .run. The full driver list is at:
installDriver.pickVersionNote: Throughout the rest of this guide, replace '<'VERSION'>' with the actual version (for example 580.95.05).
installDriver.firstPassBody: Run the installer. The option below can disable nouveau if necessary; installation may need a reboot before it can finish:
installDriver.secondPassBody: After the host comes back, run the installer again to compile and install the kernel module:
installDriver.modulesAddBody: Add the NVIDIA modules needed for host/LXC use. VFIO modules are for VM passthrough and are not required for this LXC setup:
installDriver.udevBody: So that /dev/nvidia* device nodes are created when the modules load:

persistence.heading: 3. NVIDIA driver persistence service
persistence.body: The persistence daemon keeps the GPU initialized when no other application is using it. This reduces repeated initialization latency and preserves GPU-initialization state between clients:
persistence.installCode:
cd /opt/nvidia
git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-persistenced.git
cd nvidia-persistenced/init
./install.sh
reboot
persistence.verifyBody: Verify the driver is loaded and the service is running after reboot:

nvenc.heading: 4. (Optional) Lift the NVENC concurrent-session limit
nvenc.body: NVENC session limits depend on the GPU model and driver version; consult NVIDIA’s support matrix rather than assuming a fixed limit by GPU generation. The keylase patch removes the software limit for supported driver versions. It can help encoding workloads such as Plex or Jellyfin transcoding.
nvenc.after: The patch must be re-applied after every driver update. The keylase repo also includes patch-fbc.sh for the FBC (frame buffer capture) limit if you need it.

lxcSetup.heading: 5. Configure an LXC container to use the GPU
lxcSetup.identifyNote: Note the major numbers — they vary between systems. Typical values:
lxcSetup.editBody: Stop the container first if it's running. Open its config file (replace '<'CTID'>' with the container ID):
lxcSetup.editConfigBody: Comment out any pre-existing lxc.cgroup2.devices.allow or /dev/dri lines that conflict, then append the NVIDIA wiring (adjust the major numbers to match what ls -l /dev/nv* showed on your host):
lxcSetup.editConfigCode:
lxc.cgroup2.devices.allow: c 195:* rwm
lxc.cgroup2.devices.allow: c 509:* rwm
lxc.mount.entry: /dev/nvidia0 dev/nvidia0 none bind,optional,create=file
lxc.mount.entry: /dev/nvidiactl dev/nvidiactl none bind,optional,create=file
lxc.mount.entry: /dev/nvidia-uvm dev/nvidia-uvm none bind,optional,create=file
lxc.mount.entry: /dev/nvidia-modeset dev/nvidia-modeset none bind,optional,create=file
lxc.mount.entry: /dev/nvidia-uvm-tools dev/nvidia-uvm-tools none bind,optional,create=file
lxcSetup.installCtHeading: 5.3 Install the driver inside the container
lxcSetup.installCtCalloutBody: This part runs inside the container, not on the host.
lxcSetup.installCtBody: The kernel module is already loaded by the host — the container only needs the userland libraries that match the same driver version:
lxcSetup.installCtAfter: Review the prompts and keep this installation limited to user-space libraries. Do not build or install a kernel module inside the LXC.
lxcSetup.verifyCtAfter: You should see the GPU listed and the device nodes mounted into the container's filesystem.
lxcSetup.workloadHeading: 5.5 Confirm a real workload picks up the GPU
lxcSetup.workloadBody: Enable NVIDIA hardware acceleration in Plex or Jellyfin, start a video transcode and check its dashboard or logs for actual GPU use. Installing the driver alone does not enable acceleration in the application.
lxcSetup.workloadImage2Alt: Plex using NVIDIA GPU - active session
lxcSetup.repeatNote: Repeat section 5 for each additional container that needs GPU access. Keep the user-space driver libraries in every container aligned when the host driver is updated.

docker.heading: 6. (Optional) NVIDIA Docker inside an LXC
docker.body: If Docker already runs inside the LXC, install nvidia-container-toolkit there to expose the GPU to its Docker containers. GPU access from the LXC must work first. The following commands are for a rootful Docker installation:
docker.code:
apt-get update
apt-get install -y ca-certificates curl gnupg
curl -fsSL https://nvidia.github.io/libnvidia-container/gpgkey | gpg --dearmor --yes -o /usr/share/keyrings/nvidia-container-toolkit-keyring.gpg
curl -fsSL https://nvidia.github.io/libnvidia-container/stable/deb/nvidia-container-toolkit.list | sed 's#deb https://#deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/nvidia-container-toolkit-keyring.gpg] https://#g' > /etc/apt/sources.list.d/nvidia-container-toolkit.list
apt-get update
apt-get install -y nvidia-container-toolkit
nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=docker
systemctl restart docker
docker.after: These commands configure NVIDIA’s repository, install the toolkit, configure the Docker runtime and restart Docker. LXC device permissions and cgroup restrictions still apply; verify GPU use with a test workload.

troubleshoot.heading: Troubleshooting
items: nvidia-smi works on the host but reports "No devices found" in the container: check device mounts, permissions and matching driver libraries. If versions differ, install the host’s '<'VERSION'>' in the container with --no-kernel-module.

Driver compilation fails: inspect the build log. "No precompiled kernel interface was found" can simply mean the installer must compile locally. Install headers matching uname -r using apt-get install pve-headers-$(uname -r), or the equivalent proxmox-headers package for that kernel.

NVENC sessions remain limited: confirm the patch supports the active driver. A driver update can overwrite it. For a supported version, reapply ./patch.sh from /opt/nvidia/nvidia-patch and review its output.

GPU stops responding after idle: check systemctl status nvidia-persistenced and enable the service if intended. Also inspect kernel and driver logs; a stopped persistence daemon is not the only possible cause.

Container starts but ls /dev/nv* shows no NVIDIA devices: check the bind-mount entries and host device paths. Use ls -l /dev/nv* on the host to verify NVIDIA major numbers, then check the lxc.cgroup2.devices.allow rules and permissions.
